summary: Describes a compression method for TLS using a lossless algorithm, DEFLATE, in addition to the default of no compression. TLS can negotiate compression during the handshake and apply it in the record protocol. It was updated by RFC 8447 and RFC 8996.

eli5.summary: Before locking a package, you squish it to be smaller. This lets secure connections shrink their data before sending it.

questions: how does tls deflate compression work
what is the deflate compression method in tls
what compression method values does tls reserve

subtitle: Gives TLS a standard compression method (DEFLATE) and a numbering scheme for adding more.

tldr.problem: TLS could negotiate compression, but only the 'no compression' method was standardized, so implementers had no interoperable way to compress data inside TLS.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns identifier 1 to a stateful DEFLATE compression method, splits the one-byte method number space into three zones, and sets rules for session resumption.
tldr.outcome: TLS implementations gained a shared compression method. The RFC was later updated by RFC 8447 and RFC 8996, and it warns that compression can leak information about encrypted data through its length.

today: RFC 3749 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8447 and RFC 8996, so read it together with those documents. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Compress Inside TLS
sections.content:
The Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol, as defined in RFC 2246, can negotiate a lossless data compression method in its Handshake Protocol and then apply it in its Record Protocol. But TLS only defined one standard method, CompressionMethod.null, which means no compression.

That kept implementations interoperable but left implementers without a shared way to compress. The RFC points out that TLS is used for long-lived connections that can move thousands or millions of octets, and that XML tends to be verbose. Compression is one way to cut bandwidth and latency while keeping TLS security services.

The document adds one compression method. Standardizing the compressed data formats and algorithms behind it is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Secure connections could already squish their messages in theory, but nobody agreed on how. This RFC picks one squishing method everybody can use.

sections.title: Compression Method Identifiers
sections.content:
TLS defines enum { null(0), (255) } CompressionMethod;, which leaves room for up to 256 compression methods. This RFC splits the values into three zones:

  • 0 through 63 (0x3F): reserved for IETF Standards Track protocols.
  • 64 (0x40) through 223 (0xDF): reserved for assignment to non-Standards Track methods.
  • 224 (0xE0) through 255 (0xFF): reserved for private use.

It also assigns an identifier to DEFLATE, so the definition becomes enum { null(0), DEFLATE(1), (255) } CompressionMethod;.
sections.eli5: Think of numbered coat hooks. The low hooks are for official methods, the middle hooks are for other methods, and the top hooks are for anyone's private use.

sections.title: DEFLATE and Stateful Compression
sections.content:
TLS is a stateful protocol. A compression method can be stateful (the compressor keeps its state across all compressed records) or stateless (each record is compressed on its own). The RFC notes there seems to be little known benefit in a stateless method within TLS. The DEFLATE method here is stateful, and the RFC RECOMMENDS that future methods be stateful too.

DEFLATE is described in RFC 1951. It lets the sender pick among options that trade compression ratio, speed and memory, and the receiving decompressor MUST adjust automatically to what the sender chose. All data submitted for compression MUST appear in the compressed output, with nothing held back for a later payload. Flushing ensures every compressed packet payload can be decompressed completely.

Compression can sometimes expand data. A method that exceeds the expansion limits in section 6.2.2 of RFC 2246 MUST NOT be used with TLS.
sections.eli5: The squisher remembers what it already squished, so it can do a better job as the conversation goes on. The listener has to follow whatever squishing settings the sender picked.

sections.title: History and Session Resumption
sections.content:
Keeping compression history across packets gives a higher ratio than compressing each packet alone, but one packet may then hold data needed to decompress another. That requires a reliable link and sequenced delivery. Because TLS and the layers below it provide both, compression history MAY be kept if the method supports it.

TLS also lets several connections share one session through resumption. That has operational effects: for example, load balancers would need extra state if compression state were not cleared on resumption. So two rules MUST be followed when resuming a session:

  • The compression algorithm MUST be retained.
  • The compression state and history MUST be cleared.
sections.eli5: When you come back to a conversation you paused, you keep using the same squishing method, but you forget everything the squisher remembered and start fresh.

sections.title: IANA Registry Rules
sections.content:
The RFC describes a registry of compression method identifiers maintained by the IANA, including the DEFLATE assignment. Values 0 to 63 are assigned by Standards Action, values 64 to 223 by Specification Required, and values 224 to 255 are reserved for Private Use, using the terms from RFC 2434.

The RFC also notes that the identifiers are machine-readable numbers, so human internationalization and localization issues are not introduced.
sections.eli5: A librarian keeps the official list of numbers. Official methods need a formal process, other methods need a written description, and the top numbers are free for anyone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it does not alter the threat model addressed by TLS, and the security considerations of RFC 2246 still apply. But combining compression with encryption can reveal information. Data that is the same length before compression may differ in length afterwards, so an observer who sees the compressed length may learn something about the original data.

Ciphersuites differ in how much they hide length. Stream cipher encryption without padding hides it not at all, while Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) with padding hides some, depending on how padding is chosen. Use of TLS compression SHOULD take into account that compressed length may leak more than the original length.

Compression algorithms are complex and prone to implementation errors, and a buffer overrun is a risk where the language or operating system gives no protection. Rogue data can also be built to expand to an enormous size. RFC 2246 limits this: compression has to be lossless, the allowed content length increase is limited to 1,024 bytes, and total content length is limited to 2^14 bytes.
sections.eli5: If someone can see how big your squished package is, they may guess what is inside. Also, a trick package could unsquish into something huge, so there are size limits.
